->**Hermetic Philosophy**<-
<note>original: "PHILOSOPHIA HERMETICA." The term refers to a tradition of esoteric knowledge attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, blending alchemy, astrology, and theurgy.</note>

The center of the page features a printed emblem rich in symbolic imagery:
An oval green border is formed by an **Ouroboros**—a serpent devouring its own tail—representing the eternal cycle of life, death, and the unity of all things. Within this circle, a white **pelican** is depicted "in her piety," a traditional symbol where the mother bird feeds her young with blood from her own breast. In an alchemical context, this signifies the "nourishing" of the Great Work through sacrifice and purification.

The bird perches above a square shield or pedestal featuring four red roses arranged around a central cross—the primary emblem of the **Rosicrucians** <term>Rosicrucian: A mystical secret society of the early 17th century claiming to possess secret wisdom from the ancient past</term>. From the top of the oval, a golden sun radiates light downward, symbolizing divine illumination.

# Warning to the Reader.

Be warned, dear reader, you who come across this little book, that you do not take offense at the **simplicity** <note>The German word *Einfalt* implies a plain, unadorned, or humble style, contrasting with the flowery academic language of the era.</note> of the words in this book, for beneath such simplicity lie hidden very high **mysteries**: <note>Original: *Geheimnüssen*. In mystical traditions, these are spiritual truths experienced through the heart rather than just the intellect.</note> Just as **Christ our Lord** himself spoke the great mysteries of the Kingdom of God with simple parables, and not with grand words fashioned according to the *style* <note>original: *Stylo*</note> of this world; and of this **St. Paul** also boasts: namely, that he conducted his sermons not with high and clever worldly wisdom, but with the demonstration of the Spirit and power. He also says: the **Kingdom of God** consists not in words, but in power. And such writings—because they proceed from the Spirit of God, which far surpasses all fleshly, heathen eloquence—

This likely refers to the "Friend of God from the Oberland" who famously challenged the mystic Johannes Tauler.</note>. For previously he was a great theorist and brawler <note>original: Theoreticus und Zäncker; someone more interested in abstract doctrine and arguing than in lived faith.</note>, indeed a subtle disputant <note>original: subtilis Disputator</note> and eloquent orator <note>original: beredsamer Perorator</note>, such that he focused his theology on such bickering. From the pulpit, like another Cicero <note>A famous Roman statesman and orator known for his persuasive, artistic speech.</note>, he orated with wonderful (yet carnal) eloquence concerning the high mysteries of God. 

However, such preaching—originating from a carnal, high-minded, and impure heart that did not yet know itself—did not "taste" right to the aforementioned layman. Instead, <unclear>this</unclear> layman went to him and rebuked him, saying that he was still a Pharisee <note>In this context, a "Pharisee" refers to a religious leader who possesses the "letter" of the law but lacks the "spirit," or one who teaches others what they do not practice themselves.</note> because he had never personally walked the path he showed to others. For inwardly he was struck with heavy, hard trials of the soul <note>original: Seelen-Anfechtungen; a specific term for intense spiritual anxiety, doubt, or "dark nights of the soul" viewed as a divine test.</note>, so that he

Test rather / what this man writes in this book in the light of the Spirit of God / and follow the same: Would to God / would to God / that all teachers in Christendom / might write from such light as this teacher / and might teach from such experience: Yes, would to God that in this day and age those / who wish to be leaders of the blind / would allow themselves to be enlightened more by the light of the Spirit / than by the will-o'-the-wisps <note>original: "Irrwischen," referring to deceptive marsh-lights or delusions</note> of pagan art <note>original: "Heydnischen Kunst," likely referring to secular philosophy or scholastic logic disconnected from spiritual experience</note> / and of those writers / whose souls have already been burning in the abyss for several hundred years; then things would fare better in Christendom.

Consider this well / dear reader / and set yourself to it / with preceding and zealous prayer / for the Spirit of understanding / for the reading of this scripture / with a heart / that does not seek words / human art / and [secular] science / but rather the exercise of your soul / and your perceptible improvement: If not / then simply stay away from it / and seek instead among those like yourself / for art and wind <note>original: "Kunst und Wind," an expression for vanity or empty intellectualism</note>. Lüneburg, January 12, 1644.

# DR. JOHANNES TAULER’S
## Divine Teaching / on the Virtues and the State of Highest Perfection.

### CHAPTER I.

### On the Gravity of Sins, and how we should come to the lovely Union with GOD through true Repentance.

Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near, etc. <note>original: "Thut Buß/ dann das Himmelreich ist nahe herbey kommen." This is the opening of the ministry of Jesus as found in Matthew 4:17.</note>
Our faithful Lord Jesus Christ (who has sufficiently shown us the nearest way to eternal salvation through his holy life, commandment, and teaching in the holy Gospel) began his preaching ministry with these words: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.

---

<header>THE MARROW OF THE SOUL. 25</header> <note>original Latin title: "MEDULLA ANIMÆ." This collection, though attributed to Tauler, often drew from a variety of mystical sources to provide the "marrow" or core of spiritual life.</note>
<sig>B v</sig>

If we are ever to be saved, it is necessary above all else that we perform repentance <term>Repentance: The German "Buße" carries the weight of both internal "change of heart" and the outward "penance" or amendment of life.</term> and never cease the improvement of our lives during this time, for no one lives without sin. Now it is to be noted here that one cannot perform true repentance unless one first knows how to rightly weigh the gravity of sins.

A sinner does GOD such incomprehensibly great dishonor and shame, and to himself such great, immeasurable, and ruinous harm, that if he truly recognized it, he would intentionally never commit the slightest sin for the sake of heaven or earth or everything within them; indeed, he would much rather allow himself to suffer a new death every single day. For sin is a separation from GOD, a turning toward vain creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any created thing or worldly object that a person prizes above the Creator.</note>, a defilement of the soul, a dying of the spirit, a snare of the enemy, a loss of time, a deprivation of God’s grace, of all virtues, and of eternal salvation. Sin is a distress of the conscience, a darkening of the understanding, a perversion of the will, a restlessness of the heart, and an instability of the senses.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Tauler's "Divine Teaching," opening with the necessity of repentance as the first step toward union with God. It defines sin not just as a mistake, but as a catastrophic spiritual state that separates the soul from its Creator and destabilizes the human psyche.</summary>

For the more kindhearted **GOD** is toward him / the more highly he estimates his own trespass against Him. # ->DR. JOHANNES TAULER<-
<note>original: "D. Joh. Tauleri". Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361) was a German Dominican mystic. His "Medulla Animae" (The Marrow of the Soul) is a collection of his teachings on the inner life.</note>

...is, the faster **GOD** forgives them. For even if a mother might forget her own child, **God**, according to His promise, can by no means forget us.

His mercy is so great that no flax burns as quickly in a great fire as **GOD** is ready to forgive the sinner of their sin, provided they are heartily sorry for it from the bottom of their heart. For between the goodness of **God** and the repentant sinner, there is no time or intermediary <note>Tauler emphasizes that reconciliation is instantaneous and requires no middleman once the heart is truly turned to God.</note>. A perfect reconciliation occurs between **GOD** and him, as if the sin had never been committed. **GOD** is so good that He will never again—as long as the person perseveres in a good life—impute to them that which He has once completely forgiven.

Now know that no practice is more powerful for killing sin, along with its punishment, than this aforementioned repentance. ### Chapter II.

## On the Harm of Daily Sins, and by what means we may avoid all sins.

Even if we cannot see or recognize all our daily <note>original: "tägliche Sünden." In the theology of Tauler’s time, these are "venial sins"—smaller, everyday failings that do not completely break one’s relationship with God, unlike "mortal" sins.</note> sins, we can nevertheless, through the grace of God, quite well prevent ourselves from falling into them frequently or intentionally. For daily sins blind the eyes of the soul so that one cannot see God within them, just as a dark mist blinds the eyes of the body. They consume the heat of Divine Love; they cause prayer to be heard less easily than when one guards against them; they stain the soul so that the Holy Spirit is grieved and the evil spirit rejoices; they make God a stranger to the soul as long as one does not improve; they draw a person into falling into greater sins; and they weaken the powers of the soul so that they cannot resist evil inclinations

<column-break/>

41
THE MARROW OF THE SOUL. <note>original: "MEDULLA ANIMÆ."</note>

resist; they make a person sluggish toward what is good and pull one’s desires down toward temporal things. <insert>~~they cause a great purgatory and for a long time prevent the contemplation of God.~~</insert> <note>This sentence has been struck through with horizontal ink lines in the original manuscript, likely by a later editor or reader seeking to remove Catholic doctrines like Purgatory from the text.</note> Now see whether the harm is small—especially when these sins happen knowingly or out of bad habit.

Now there are six parts through which a person may live daily in the grace of God without any mortal sins, as long as he keeps them.

The <gloss>first</gloss> is when a person is protected by Divine power, and all his powers are strengthened through the grace of God. God had created Adam. But when the lower powers turned away from the highest powers, he fell at that very hour. Likewise, if we turn toward sensuality without the permission of Higher Discretion <note>original: "Bescheidenheit." But if we turn outward and do something with the permission of true discretion, then we do not fall; however, such a person must be well-enlightened by God and humble, so that they might not be deceived.

The third way is when the human will is entirely closed and subjected to the Will of God, and if a person always perceives God’s will in their speech and thereafter lives without their own will—such a person may not sin.

The fourth way is when a person directs all things toward the mean <note>original: "Mittel." The fifth way is when a person is poor both internally and externally; for the poor always stand in suffering. When a failing then falls upon them, the suffering is immediately present, and they digest it at once in the stomach of poverty.

The sixth way is this: when a person’s heart is set aglow with the living fire of the Holy Spirit. For the great love of God consumes all the failings of man and cleanses him from all sins. Such a person is honored and protected by the angels and by the entire heavenly host. Their prayer is pure and is heard by God; they obtain free access and friendship with God, and they receive inward peace.

### Chapter IV.

### On the Humility, Patience, and Detachment of a Person who has Died to the Self; and on Certain Signs by Which They May Test Themselves, Lest They Be Deceived.

A dead person is characterized by three things: The first is that they are lowered into the earth; the second is that they may be stepped upon with feet until the Last Day <note>The day of final judgment at the end of the world.</note>; the third is that their corpse becomes nothing. By these three points, one may also recognize a person who has died to themselves <note>Tauler uses physical death as an allegory for "mortification," the spiritual process of killing off ego and selfish desires.</note>.

Firstly, a person who has died in God sinks before GOD and all people into such bottomless humility that they never again exalt themselves in their heart above any person: And they consider themselves the lowliest of all, so that they regard all people before GOD as being holier and better than themselves.

<column-break/>

<page-num>57</page-num>
<header>THE MARROW OF THE SOUL <note>original Latin: "MEDULLA ANIMÆ."</note></header>
**D v**
<meta>catchword: things</meta>

Secondly, they suffer with patient **detachment** <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; the state of being surrendered to God's will regardless of outward circumstances.</note> that they be walked upon with feet until the Last Day; that is, that until their final end, they will endure and bear all adversity, shame, disgrace, suffering, and pain, whether it comes from GOD or from **creatures** <note>original: "Creaturen"; meaning any created thing or being, such as other people, animals, or nature, as opposed to the Creator.</note>, whether it happens to them rightly or wrongly. They shall not defend themselves, nor excuse themselves, nor complain; nor shall they desire to take revenge, but rather they are just like a dead person in the grave, subject to all things. Whether one does them good or evil, love or sorrow, whether one praises or slanders them, it is all one to them, and they remain entirely untouched, without any vengeance.

Thirdly, they have become nothing in everything that is not GOD; for they have turned themselves entirely toward GOD, and all temporal and bodily things in their desire shall be dead: Whether GOD gives to them or GOD takes from them, they stand entirely alone, surrendered in GOD. They take only the necessities from created things, which nature cannot do without, and have given their will captive into the will of God, and let go of themselves and all...

<summary>Tauler uses the metaphor of a corpse to describe the three hallmarks of spiritual maturity: profound humility, the patient endurance of mistreatment without retaliation, and the total surrender of personal will to God.</summary>

But so that a person is not led astray on this path, but rather that Nature and Grace may work together in harmony: one must take note of three points. Whoever stands firmly in these cannot easily be deceived by **false freedom**, **natural light**, or **false prophets**. They may well cause a stumbling block in the soul's foundation <note>original: "Grund." ### Chapter V.

### Concerning several obstacles, and conversely, several elements that serve toward great perfection.

The **first** thing by which God and His grace are greatly hindered within us is an unrestrained nature, which clings inordinately with love and desire to **creatures** <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any "created thing"—including people, objects, or status—rather than just animals.</note>, or created things. These people are easily moved by the love and sorrow of temporal and accidental things; therefore, they lose the love of God and remain **unmortified** <note>original: "unerstorben." In mystical theology, this refers to a person who has not yet "died" to their worldly desires and ego.</note>.

The **second** is self-love <note>original: "engene Liebe," literally "narrow love" or "own-love."</note>, self-will, self-mindedness, and self-seeking; this often causes unrest and distraction of the heart. For whoever does not seek and love God above all things and above themselves is not worthy of God's honor, of all virtues, nor of God the Lord Himself; for such a person is always inclined toward their own profit, honor, and pleasure, and is easily overcome by manifold

The **fourth** is that they are hasty and bold, and do not heed small failings; through this, they lose the peace and purity of the heart.

The **fifth** is that they very easily exalt themselves with self-satisfaction and personal opinion because of good works—which do not even belong to them <note>Tauler emphasizes that good works come from God's grace, not the individual's merit.</note>—and desire, out of a proud foundation, to be esteemed by people. With this, they lose true humility and are often forsaken by God.

The **sixth** is that they very easily judge what they see and hear, and carry an evil suspicion and ill-will toward their neighbor; with this, they lose brotherly love.

The **ninth** is that they perform all their works more out of habit than out of an inward drive. They pay more attention to the specific ways, the size, and the variety of good works than to a pure intention and fiery love for God. Therefore, they do not realize how God lives in them with the fullness of His grace.

The **third**: He should bear a universal love toward all people, regard all people as his brothers, and speak of them—both in their presence and in their absence—in the same way.

The **fourth**: He should receive all things from God alone, and offer them back to God along with all created things. He should dedicate all things to God as an eternal sacrifice and an eternal praise; then God will answer him, and he will find peace in all things.

### CHAPTER VI <note>original Latin: "CAPUT VI."</note>

#### A chain / both of sins / as well as of virtues.

Since the Lord God is now in [us] / and much closer to us / than we are to ourselves: Why then do we not feel Him within us? It is because His grace cannot work in us. Why then does His grace not work in us? Because we do not inwardly desire it with a humble heart. Why do we not desire it with a humble heart? ### Chapter VII.

### How man should return to his origin / which is God / and overcome all failings.

A person / who wishes to be freed from sins / to walk in the way of virtue / and to attain his salvation / and also to grow within it / should diligently observe and practice the following teachings and points.

### CHAPTER X. <note>original: "C A P U T X."</note>

#### Further concerning true humility / and how it gives birth to the denial of self.

<summary>Tauler explains that patient suffering and "yieldedness" (Gelassenheit) bring a soul to perfection faster than a year of good works, citing Christ's silent endurance as the ultimate model. ### CHAPTER XII.

# Of inward, highest yieldedness, and the vanishing of the self in GOD.

Up to this point, we have spoken of the yieldedness <term>Gelassenheit: a core concept in German mysticism referring to a state of letting go, detachment from the self, and total surrender to God's will</term> that belongs to the soul, in the manner in which it gives life to the body; and this is called an outward yieldedness.

Now follows the inward yieldedness, which belongs to the spirit, whose work does not touch the body. Its works are pure, and beyond all names, directed beyond time toward the incorporeal and uncreated Good, which is GOD himself. There, the spirit of man is drawn upward and stretched out with all its powers; it works in supernatural power, sees in supernatural light, burns in the supernatural love of GOD, and touches the clearest, most detached substance. There, it does not shine into time, but rests in eternity,

<meta>catchword: entirely</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>133</page-num>
<header>MARROW OF THE SOUL. 133</header>

entirely and utterly sunk away from itself. It has also nakedly and purely fallen away from all that it is capable of—from all that it is, all that it can do, knows, loves, has, possesses, beholds, or uses. That is to say: the spirit has fallen away, sunken, lost, and denied itself, even unto a state of non-stirring <note>original: "Nichtregen" — a state of perfect stillness or lack of self-driven movement</note>, not living for itself, not being fit for its own purposes, and having no power of its own. This occurs in this yieldedness of the clear spirit, within the bottomless abyss of the Godhead.

To speak of this high inward yieldedness, all tongues are too meager. And they may well say: "Ah, ah, ah, Lord GOD," as Jeremiah spoke: "I cannot speak, for I am a child" <note>Referencing Jeremiah 1:6, where the prophet expresses his inadequacy before the divine</note>. Yet this yieldedness is possible because of God's unfathomable dominion, for He can do all things; but among many saints who practice their faith on earth, there are few who are drawn into a true, undeceived ground <term>Grund: the "ground" of the soul is the deepest, most essential part of a person where they can meet God directly</term> in this matter. The reason for this is that they stand upon their own opinions and live in self-love. But all who intend to penetrate into this clear ground must necessarily cast off all self-love. For self-love is a great, clumsy burden, which—

This state requires the total abandonment of self-will and self-love, which Tauler views as the primary obstacles to divine union.</summary>

This refers to the "Divine Play," a common mystical concept describing the dynamic, joyful, and non-toilsome interaction between the soul and God.</note> of GOD, which the spirit prepares in the recognition of the highest food. For the more and more GOD shows and reveals Himself to it in this clear light, the hungrier and more desirous the spirit becomes for the Godhead, whether this happens knowingly or unknowingly. But the more it hungers for the Godhead, the more GOD desires to fill the empty **ground** <term>Grund: the soul’s deepest essence</term>.

Here is an infinite circle, in which the knowing is hungry in the fulfilling, and in the hunger is fulfilled. Beyond this, there is also in this circle a wonderful rational circle; for GOD becomes a willing understanding to the spirit, in that He makes Himself measurable and comprehensible in a supernatural light, and allows Himself [to be found] in the rational circle—that is, in the movement...

### ->DR. JOHN TAULER / MARROW OF THE SOUL<-
<meta>Signature: K iv</meta>

A servant of God does not desire that one tells him or commands him what he gladly hears; rather, he desires to hear what one wishes to say or command to him. Now know further, that many parts belong to perfect obedience: Firstly, he should be wise and discreet <note>In this context, "discreet" (German: *bescheiden*) refers to the ability to discern or judge rightly between different options.</note>, so that he knows what is commanded or forbidden—provided it is not against God and His commandments.

But in all other things, whether it be fasting, keeping watch, praying, working, or whatever it may be: the more one exists in simple obedience, the better that obedience is.

Secondly, it should be plain <note>original: "schlecht." In Tauler's time, this meant "straightforward" or "simple," rather than "bad" or "poor" as it does in modern German.</note> and simple; that is, solely for the honor of God, and not for the sake of any personal gain, whether in time or eternity. One may well desire eternal life, but the more sincere and pure the obedience is for the sake of God’s honor, the better and sweeter it is.

For to be obedient purely for the honor of God is the most necessary thing, and belongs to the children, but not to the servants or hirelings <note>original: "Miedlingen." This refers to those who perform spiritual duties only for a reward or "pay," rather than out of love.</note>; for the honor of the Father tastes better to them than any reward, and they increase more through a single work than the hirelings do in a thousand years who serve God for a reward.

<column-break/>

<page-num>151</page-num>
Obedience should also be joyful, for God loves a cheerful giver, and forced service does not please Him. If you wish to be joyfully obedient, then learn to love much; for love makes all works easy, so that they seem too small to the person to offer up to their Most Beloved.

Obedience is also quick, for it does not delay in doing good, but is immediately ready for it; the person finds within themselves a greater inclination to do that which they are told to do, rather than that which they have chosen for themselves. And because he finds that a small work done out of obedience is more pleasing to his Beloved than a great work done out of self-will <note>original: "Eygenwilligkeit." This is a central theme in Tauler's mysticism: the need to replace the "ego-will" with the Divine will.</note>: so he desires at all times to "go out" of himself, so that he may belong entirely to God.

Obedience is also manly <note>In the sense of being courageous, steadfast, or spiritually strong.</note>; whatever he is commanded, he stands by it with a strong spirit, such that almost no thing can be too difficult for him. And if he could do everything alone, it would seem a small thing to him. For he is so pious and honest that he forgets everything he has done, or might do, and looks only to what is required of him, that he might do it, and desires to do more.

## **Chapter XIV.**

### **Of the Forsaking of One's Own Will.**

Upon obedience follows the forsaking of one's own will and one's own opinion <note>original: "Gutdüncken." Refers to one's personal judgment or what "seems good" to the individual rather than what God wills.</note>. For no one can forsake his own will and let himself be guided by another's will: for a ges- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "geschwinder" (faster/more agile) or "gesunder" (healthier).</note>

The relinquishing of one's own will, or **Gelassenheit** <note>original: "Gelassenheit." Who then is a self-willed person <note>original: "eigen Mensch." Therefore, he never has peace or performs truly good works; even what he does brings him no inward satisfaction, for he is not yet capable of receiving the grace of **God**, and he is preoccupied with choosing this or that. One moment he wants to experience something great and have a powerful turning toward **God** and be well-off in it; the next moment he wants to be a poor man, or be in a **hermit's cell** <note>original: "Klausen."</note>, or in a better congregation, and all these things seem good to him. ### CHAPTER XV <note>original: "CAPUT XV"</note>

### On Patience and all Suffering, after the Example of Christ, and all the Saints.

From the surrender <term>surrender: "Gelassenheit," the mystical practice of letting go of one's own will and desires to be fully available to God</term> of one’s own will, patience arises. 
   Now know, that patience is a virtue which can bear all suffering and adversity, whether it be persecution or scorn, with an equal mind: Patience means as much as a work of peace, for it is impossible that anyone can have peace without singular patience. This virtue is a medicine for all sickness. And although the flesh is humbled in many ways, the patient spirit nevertheless remains at rest, as Christ says: Possess your soul in patience. <note>original: "Possidete animas vestras in patientia vestra," from Luke 21:19</note> The patience of man also greatly sweetens the pain and agony of the body; for the more impatient and unwilling he is in his soul, the more he also [torments] <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "peiniget" indicates the sentence concludes with "torments" on the next page.</note> in his body—

Dear soul, look and see how great is the misdeed we have committed against the one who is the supreme **Lord** alone, and without whom nothing exists; He who is not only an example of our patience, but also the crown of our victory. For He does not wish for us to suffer in vain; rather, He wills that our suffering be richly rewarded with the fruits of His own suffering (which benefit us). We may take comfort in this much more securely than in our own suffering, for without the fruit of His suffering, no suffering of ours could be of any use.

True divine practice is never found in a person unless they have a surrendered mind, ready to suffer all things, no matter how difficult they may be, and to fulfill **GOD’s** admonition in deed, so that the beloved will of **GOD**—as much as his powers allow—may be satisfied therein.

### CHAPTER XVI.

## On internal detachment, through which we should be united with God in all works and in all places.

**W**hoever desires to lead a truly **inward** life <term>inward: the original German "eingezogen" implies a life gathered inward or "drawn in" from worldly distractions</term> must dwell in the city of Jerusalem—that is, in peace <note>The name Jerusalem was traditionally interpreted in medieval theology as "Vision of Peace."</note>—and must be without blame or mortal sins, and free from all **disordered inclinations** toward created things, whether they be of love or of sorrow. He must be able to lift up his spirit to God without hindrance, to perceive God constantly, to satisfy His promptings and admonitions, and to be inclined toward God at all times. For an inward life consists more of what is within than what is without; and just as an imperfect person must flee external things if he wishes to turn entirely toward God—and that not without great pain and labor (for the things that we possess with

For he possesses nothing with **disordered love**, and his **inward-turning** <term>inward-turning: "Einkehr," the act of retreating into the "ground of the soul" to find God</term> to God is made so ready and easy for him through love and constant practice and awareness of God, that he does not need to exert himself much. 

And although it is not easily possible to remain always expanded in God, nevertheless, when a good person becomes aware that he is inclined toward useless things, he easily and quickly turns away from them with great self-indignation, because he is so inconstant. And when he looks upon things without **attachment**, he can turn away from them without effort, for he is more inclined toward the **inward-turning** than the **outward-turning**. Indeed, one person may be by nature quieter than another, but he is not holier because of it. ## CHAPTER XVII.

### How a good person, united with God's will, is capable of all things, and concerning inward comfort and lack of comfort.

A person should attribute nothing to themselves, nor be too greatly troubled, or consider themselves far from God

Nothing can be lacking to you, if it is the case that you have a righteous, true will. If you desire to have humility, love, or other virtues, and desire it powerfully with all your will, then you have them. Neither God nor any creature can take this from you, as long as your will is a righteous, Divine will. But a Divine will is one that desires everything it wants purely for the glory of God; our will cannot do this by nature. One can recognize the Divine will no better than by this: that a person intends only the glory of God. Nothing can bind this will—neither death nor life, neither the Devil nor any creature.

One must not just say: "I want," but one must also want powerfully. If a virtue or spiritual good were over a thousand miles away, and I wanted it with a perfect will, then it would belong to me much more truly <note>original: "eigentlicher," meaning more essentially or properly mine</note> than if I had it in my lap <note>original: "Schooß"</note> against my will. # DR. JOHN TAULER

And thus, with my whole will, I might kill many people, even if I did not actually do so with works.

I do not mean to say that sin committed in deed is not greater than the will without the work. But consent completes the sin, even if it is not carried out in deed, for sin lies more in the will than in the works. Why then should I not also be capable of the same with a good will? I am capable of the same much better and incomparably more regarding the good: For God works with the good will, so that the work of the good will becomes easier; but the evil will has only its own wickedness as a helper. And as much as the grace of Almighty God can do more with the good will than the evil alone, so much is the good will more powerful through God’s grace to accomplish that which it desires, than the evil will is with its own wickedness.

### Chapter XVIII.

## How a person should conduct 
## themselves in the temptation 
## of vices.

Temptation and the inclination toward vice never happen in good people without great fruit and progress. There are two kinds of good people: These are of such a nature that no failing, or very little, strikes them. Others are tempted outwardly in the presence of the causes of failings, and are then moved toward sins, such as anger, vain glory, greed, unchastity, or whatever it may be; but with their <term>highest powers</term> <note>In medieval psychology, the "highest powers" are the intellect and the will, which can remain fixed on God even when the lower, sensory emotions (the "lower powers") are agitated</note> they stand entirely free and unmoved, so that they do not consent to such failings; they do not want to be angry, to exalt themselves, or any other

Also, the movement of **vice** brings **virtue** into the **mind** <term>Gemüt</term><note>A key term in German mysticism referring to the seat of the soul’s powers—the inner disposition or heart.</note>, and awakens us to be more earnest in the **service of GOD**, and to take heed of **GOD** and ourselves, and to exercise ourselves at all times in **virtues**. Taking close heed of the **inclination** toward **vice** admonishes and strengthens us in **virtue**; for the weaker we recognize and find ourselves to be, the more we should take heed of the **blessings** and **grace of GOD**. For both **virtue** and **vice** depend upon our **will**.

Furthermore, one should hold oneself as if in a dormant state amidst all influences, whether they be in the spirit or in nature, and not take for oneself as much as a hair’s breadth of it, nor ever hold onto it with one's own perception or observation. Instead, one should sink into a simple, humble, and lovely peace, and in a resigned <term>releasement</term> <note>original: *Gelassenheit*; a central concept in German mysticism referring to a state of total surrender and letting go of self-will to be open to God.</note>, in an <term>un-becoming</term> <note>original: *entwerden*; the process of the self ceasing to be its own center of gravity or "undoing" the ego.</note>, in a true, pure, and naked poverty of oneself and of all things—a poverty that contains nothing—and into that same poverty one should also sink or un-become.

The **seed** cannot bring forth the **tree**, nor the **flower** the **fruit**, unless they first deny themselves and die and lose themselves entirely.

Who was ever so wise that he could find the tree in the seed, or the fruit in the flower? It is all distant and foreign, and the more the fruit grows and increases, the more the flower passes away,

withers, and spoils. So also, certainly in truth, whoever dies most to what is his own and to himself, grows most surely and fruitfully in **GOD**. This pure intending of **GOD** never fails or rejects **GOD**, whether it is consciously thought or not, prayed or not, or in whatever manner it occurs.

To intend **GOD** is not to intend **GOD** only when He is felt in His presence, nor is it to intend one's own benefit. Alas, what lies hidden in <term>nature</term> <note>In this context, Tauler uses "nature" to mean the fallen human instinct that is inherently selfish and seeks its own comfort.</note>, which always seeks and intends its own gain in all things! # CHAPTER XXIII.
## How we are to become one with Christ / and how we should walk in Heaven.

St. Paul says: *I know a man in Christ* <note>original: "Ich kenne einen Menschen in Christo" — a reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where Paul speaks of a mystical experience.</note>: This word is understood by few people / what it means to be "one in Christ" / for this requires <term>detachment</term> <note>original: "Gelassenheit" — a key term in German mysticism meaning a total letting go of self-will and worldly attachments to become receptive to God.</note> from everything that is not (One) / and anything of that sort / and in whatever way this one thing has any other focus outside of Christ: whether the person be in their outward or inward state. And every one / even the one who is the lowest / would not wish to be the highest.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

# How one should begin properly / and rise up in a good and inward spiritual life / also in what manner one should be silent and speak.

There are three pieces / which make a good person:

The first: A good person must have a pure, clean conscience / without the accusation of mortal sins. It is no wonder when they come to **GOD** that they then remain and are completely unlike the internal friends of **GOD**. But an internal person must stand very carefully on his guard, so that he lets nothing foreign join with him that might be dissimilar or alien to this state, whether it be images, thoughts, or any kind of multiplicity <note>original: "Mannigfaltigkeit"—the state of being distracted by many worldly things instead of focusing on the One</note> from without or within. For if a person loses this gift of **GOD**, it often happens that he is cast into great darkness, into dryness <term>dryness: "Dürre," a common mystical term (aridity) for a period where one feels no spiritual comfort or emotion</term>, and into an insensibility that falls upon him, resulting in a distaste for all good exercises of virtue. He does not know what is Divine, for it is a pain and a torment to him; he cannot stretch himself out, expand, or sink himself into **GOD**, and he does not know how he should prepare himself for it. 

In this state, the person should endure in lovely patience: for all is not lost because of this. Rather, the faithful Father permits it out of great love, to preserve the person, so that henceforth he might be all the more careful on his guard. # DR. JOHN TAULER

Now see what those people neglect who live recklessly and without a thought for eternity. ### ->Chapter XXX.<-
<note>original: "Caput XXX."</note>

->**Many reasons why we should love our enemies from the heart.**<-

Our dear Lord Jesus Christ allowed Judas, His mortal enemy, to walk with Him for seven reasons.

The first: He wished at all times to have that same person before His eyes who would deliver Him into death, so that His passion <note>original: "Passion" — the suffering of Christ leading up to the crucifixion.</note> and torment <note>original: "Marter" — physical or spiritual torture.</note> would be renewed at all times. For just as He well knew His passion in His Divine, eternal wisdom, so He also wished to never forget His pain before His human eyes; therefore, it was renewed for Him at all times in this life.

The second is: He wished to prove with deeds what He taught us with words: to love enemies just as well as friends.

The third is: That He might teach us how we

### C H A P T E R XXXIII.

### How we should seek God in our soul, and trust in Him.

The person who lacks **God**, and does not examine his own soul, should not rest until he finds Him again in his **inner spirit**. <note>The German term "Gemüt" refers to the seat of the soul’s powers—encompassing the mind, heart, and will—where the human meets the Divine.</note> It is a great shame that a good person is ever found in a state where **God** is not present in his mind. He should consider it the greatest shame to seek comfort, or anything at all, in any **creature**, <note>In mystical theology, a "creature" refers to any created thing (people, objects, status) as opposed to the Creator.</note> except in **God** alone.

When he is well-fastened to **God** in his soul, then he walks safely wherever he goes, and does well in whatever he does; but without Him, he is never safe, regardless of where he is or whom he is with. **God** the **Lord** hides Himself somewhat; if we then seek something else and do not pay heed to Him, He goes away and remains

<column-break/>

remains away for a very long time, and provides comfort only rarely. **God** alone must be intended; he who intends anything else does not truly intend **God**. You should also not intend anything *in* **God**—neither graces, nor gifts, nor anything that one might desire—for in Him, you find everything together. Be it gifts or graces, forgiveness of sins, or the restoration of lost time—whether you have neglected your prayer, your practice, or your time, or whatever you can think of—turn back into Him alone from that very moment. That is: you should at once sink and drown in His **Divine Will**. You should accustom yourself to finding or knowing **God** almost unceasingly in your spirit—not only in your thoughts, but also when a person forgets himself so that something blameworthy falls upon his conscience; in such a case, the first and quickest **return** to **God** is the very best. Therefore, do not delay for the sake of confession, nor for prayer, nor for any other thing, but direct your conscience to **God** immediately. Unprepared and unconfessed, <note>Tauler is not dismissing the sacrament of confession, but rather emphasizing that the soul should not wait for the ritual before reconciling its heart with God.</note> flee to **God**, and confess to the priest at the proper time; **God** is not to be made bitter by our failings.

<summary>Tauler instructs the seeker to maintain an unceasing awareness of God's presence in the inner spirit, warning against seeking comfort in created things and urging an immediate, internal return to God whenever the conscience is troubled.</summary>

Therefore, here is a rest and refreshment, as David says: This is my rest from time to time. <note>original: "Diß iſt von Zeiten zu Zeiten meine Ruhe." Likely a paraphrased reference to Psalm 132:14.</note>

If God is then so much our own, so near within us, and so radiant and lovely, why is He then so unknown and far from us? This is solely the fault of our own sloth. For diligence and sharp perception of ourselves are required for this above all else. And if one then finds that they have lost it and have turned outward, then one must help oneself most of all with simple faith; for in no other way could one fall into unbelief <note>German: *Unglauben*. Could also be translated as "lack of faith" or "doubt."</note> more easily than in this lapse.

Therefore, a person should always and most readily turn back into God, and then with God into themselves; thus God alone will become a good "means" <note>Here used in the sense of a bridge or a medium through which all other things are experienced.</note> between them and all things, as He Himself says: He who [abides] in me...

<summary>Tauler explains that the highest spiritual work is "un-becoming" and detaching from transitory things to reach a state of divine "emptiness." He emphasizes that God is present in all things and places, and only human sloth and external distractions prevent us from experiencing this constant divine rest.</summary>

Learn three things well. Always be a person who is beginning—this takes away all sluggishness. Always be intimate with God—so you remain in the joy of a good conscience. ## Chapter XXXIV.

->On the images that we should contemplate,<-
->and how one may give leave to all images,<-
->and come to poverty of spirit.<-

It is a question: Whether one may give leave <note>original: *Urlaub geben*. In Tauler's vocabulary, this means to dismiss, detach from, or "say goodbye" to mental images and concepts in order to reach a state of pure contemplation.</note> to old images, and cling to God with a bare mind? Answer: One may give leave to the images in two ways. Because the truth thereby escapes me,

...departs / which every good image would have signified to me. Which are the most useful images <term>Bilder: mental representations or meditative concepts used to focus the mind on spiritual truths</term> that a person may have?

The first: That a person, with heartfelt repentance and a complete turning away [from the world], confesses his past sinful life.

The second is: That he learns to recognize our Lord’s suffering and his death out of great love. These are the most useful images, for no person can ever grow to great things unless he has first wisely passed through these images.

### Which are now the most noble images?

The first: That a person turns himself toward the high union of the Divine and Human natures <note>This refers to the "Hypostatic Union," the theological doctrine of Christ being both fully God and fully man.</note>.

The second: Toward the nobility and wealth of his own spirit and soul.

The third: Toward the worthy body of our Lord.

If these three images are well-considered, they are the most noble images. Furthermore, a person should turn himself toward the Holy Trinity of the three persons; he should contemplate how the Son is born of the Father, eternally remaining within, and from both of them—

The third is: The bottomless, essential, simple <note>In mystical German, "simple" (*einfältig*) means "uncomplicated" or "without parts," referring to the absolute unity of God.</note> being of the Godhead. This is to be pondered as far as one is able; these are the purest images.

Why should one grant leave <note>original: *Urlaub geben*. In this context, it means to dismiss, let go of, or transcend these mental images to reach a higher state of contemplation.</note> to all images? Because they are nothing but a mere path to the Truth. If I am now to come to the bare Truth, I must grant leave to the path, and pass through all good images in the right order—from the lowest to the middle to the highest—so that no Truth escapes me. For this is one of the most noble works that a person can perform here: to be rationally transformed into noble images.

By what should one recognize when to grant leave to these noble images, so that one does not dismiss them too early, and also does not remain upon them too long? By three things:

The first: When you look upon everything that you ever hear or understand with weariness <note>original: *Verdruß*. A sense of spiritual dissatisfaction or "holy boredom" that suggests the soul is ready for a deeper level of reality.</note>.

The second: That you no longer hear or understand anything that brings you any pleasure.

<summary>Tauler categorizes the mental "images" or meditative subjects a person uses to approach God, ranging from repentance to the nature of the Trinity. ### Chapter XXXV. <note>original: *Caput XXXV.*</note>

## When our will is entirely dead and lost in God.

Because much has been written before about fundamental detachment <term>Gelassenheit: a central concept in German mysticism meaning "yieldedness," "detachment," or the total surrender of the self-will to God</term> and the departure from one's own will (which is the right way to all holiness), there follow hereafter six pieces by which a person can notice whether their will is fundamentally dead and transposed into God. The first is: That a person will not commit themselves to any sinful works (small or great), but rather flees and resists them at all times, and withdraws their will from them.

Yes, even if he could understand all of Holy Scripture, and could teach other people and thereby bring them to heaven—yet all of this may not help him much if he withdraws himself from **GOD** and remains in "self-attachment" <term>Eygenschafft: a state of being possessed by one's own ego or self-will, rather than being free for God</term>, and thereby hinders himself so that he cannot joyfully turn inward and give himself entirely to **GOD**, or offer himself to His honor. For this reason all Scriptures were written: namely, that we should become, be, and remain a living, inward sacrifice for **God**.

### Chapter XXXVII. <note>original: "Caput XXXVII"</note>

### On the preparation to worthily receive the holy Sacrament, and the great grace hidden within it.

Among all the exercises a person may have, none is so noble, divine, and certain for attaining the highest Good and being inwardly united with it, as to frequently and fervently receive the worthy body of our **Lord JESUS Christ**. ### On twelve great gifts and graces which God gives to all those who receive Him worthily in the Sacrament.

The inward man receives through our **Lord's** body twelve great fruits, which are unknown to the common person and even to many spiritual people.

The second is: That the love of temporal <term>creatures</term> <note>original: "Creaturen"; in this context, it refers to any created thing—people, objects, or worldly concerns—as opposed to the Creator.</note> diminishes Divine love; for the more multifaceted and scattered such love is, the lesser is the Divine love.

The love which the soul has for creatures apart from **GOD** must necessarily be driven out, because one finds no creature that possesses all perfection entirely within itself. Since a person does not find everything in one creature, he seeks it in another.

The soul never rests until it comes to where it finds all in all—all perfection at once and undivided—and that is **GOD** alone. And although one calls upon the **Saints** for their <term>intercession</term> <note>original: "Vorbitt"; asking a saint to pray to God on one's behalf.</note> with **GOD** (because they are now one spirit with and in **GOD**, and not apart from Him), yet we should not, nor can we, rest in them as our final end, for that is **GOD** alone.

The third cause is: That the pleasure of creatures is mixed with bitterness; and if the bitterness is not outward, it is much greater inwardly. A person should much rather bear a wound on his body than allow the accusation of sins to remain within his heart.

The fourth cause is: That the creature is divided in itself; for pleasure in clothing is not the same as pleasure in food and drink. Thus it is also with spiritual things: the satisfaction of prayer is [joined] with the satisfaction of <term>inwardness</term> <note>original: "Innigkeit"; a deep, heartfelt devotion or intimacy with the divine.</note>. It is good for man that the creature has no perfection in itself; for if man had all satisfaction in creatures, he would never seek **GOD** again.

The fifth cause is: That creatures are wearisome; there is no creature so pleasant that a man could use or look upon it for so long that he would not eventually become weary of it.

Here, man must leave himself to **God** fundamentally—whether He gives to him or takes from him—so that he may be content therein.

Whoever now finds himself in such a surrendered and humble way, to freely leave himself for the honor of **God**...

When a person then remains standing still on this path until the time when it seems right to the bottomless mercy of **God** that he becomes receptive to great grace, then **God** takes him and leads him to the living fountain that has flowed eternally and still flows into all receptive hearts.

# DR. JOHN TAULER I

...have tasted droplets of this true fountain are not easily recognized, for they are quite simple <note>The original German "schlecht" here means "plain" or "uncomplicated," rather than "bad."</note> in their words and their whole being. They do not like to use many words with anyone, unless it is a matter of necessity. They are simply obedient to the holy Church, and it causes them great pain when they must speak with people who use many "free" and high-sounding words that cannot easily be refuted with Holy Scripture. Their inner eyes are opened very wide, so that they can see far and wide. And when they look around and see their fellow human beings in suffering or sin, it causes them pain out of the true compassion they have for them. From this, it is easy to notice that the "free, false person" <note>Tauler is likely critiquing the "Brethren of the Free Spirit," a contemporary movement that claimed spiritual perfection exempts one from moral laws and suffering.</note> leads the good-hearted astray by saying that they no longer need to suffer. For an upright person is inwardly terrified when **God** lets things go well for him in the luck and health of his nature. But when they find their nature under pressure, they are content, for they always have the image of **Christ** and all His true followers before their eyes.

### CHAPTER 41

### How one should obtain God's grace,
### purity, and love, etc.

IN **Christ Jesus**, I wish that you may perfectly possess the light of grace, purity of soul and body, love of the heart, and humble detachment <note>German: *Abgeschiedenheit*. This is a key term in Tauler’s theology, referring to a state of being "set apart" or "disentangled" from worldly concerns to be fully present to God.</note> in a new life in **God**. To obtain grace from **God**, there is nothing better than for a person to stand in fear before **God** at all times, and to worry that he does too little for **God** but too much for the world; whoever does this receives a new light of grace at all times.

Purity and sincerity of the soul are earned from **God** if one does not willfully remain in lustful thoughts, words, or works that are against **God**. In the person who stands thus pure, **God** builds a dwelling (**Father, Son, and**

# MARROW OF THE SOUL

**Holy Spirit**) to dwell with him with unfathomable love, and with the joys of **God** and the whole Heavenly host. Love of the heart is received from **God** with grateful recognition of the physical and spiritual gifts and benefits that **God** has ever shown to a person, and intends to show yet in eternal joy and blessedness. Through this, a person is inflamed in Divine love. ### CHAPTER 42.
## How one should kindle the fire of Divine Love.

Beloved in Christ Jesus: May the overflowing love of the Holy Spirit, in the mighty power of the Father, together with the Son’s crystal-clear wisdom, be your eternal kindler. The glow of love, which the Holy Spirit (who is also called away from the cold world) has kindled within you with Himself, desires that it remain always fiery and glowing in His Divine love, and that it permeate all the powers of your soul with unceasing intensity <note>original: *Qual*. In this mystical context, it refers to a pressing, inward labor or "agony" of longing rather than simple physical pain.</note>, with a well-ordered outward expression of the external man in both doing and refraining, in the possession and lack of all things—whether they be physical or spiritual—with true detachment <note>original: *Gelassenheit*. A key term in German mysticism referring to a state of letting go of self-will to be filled by God.</note> in the will of God. This flame of love must also always stand on guard against the false misty dew of all worldly pleasures in all things of this sorrowful world, excepting that which belongs to honest necessity according to nature.

---

# MARROW OF THE SOUL
<note>original: *MEDULLA ANIMÆ*.</note>

These flames of love must also always be pressed down <note>In the sense of banking a fire to keep it burning longer.</note> by remaining within the knowledge of the Jewel <note>original: *Kleynod*. A precious treasure or gem, here symbolizing the indwelling presence of God.</note> that is God Himself, regardless of what He has also given through all temporal and spiritual gifts, of which there are many, and which have specifically happened to you more than to many other people. Ah, ah, take good heed of this, and let it draw you especially toward God. The coal of love must also always be covered, internally and externally in all things, with the ash of good, detached, and gentle humility. # CHAPTER 43.
## On a Sinking Away from Oneself and All Things.

In Christ JESUS, I wish for you the old and the new eternally born Word, which is planted in the Divine Nature, and in turn gives birth within itself to all rational, eternal, chosen spirits who, with a clear and detached <note>original: *gelassenen*. A central term in German mysticism referring to a state of letting go of self-will to be filled by God.</note> submission, surrender themselves in all things and renounce all things except GOD, in an ascending, bottomless humility towards that overflowing and Divine Presence <note>original: *Gegenwurff*. In this context, it refers to the Divine Object or "Counter-throw" toward which the soul is directed.</note> into which all spirits cast themselves—into the single secret Essence, or the proper home of grace in Christ Jesus—for a joyful old and new year, which is called Eternity in GOD.

In Christ JESUS, I say: a pure heart full of GOD I wish for you in a hidden, inward Ground <note>original: *Grunde*. In Rhenish mysticism, the "Ground" of the soul is the deepest point where the soul meets God, beyond the reach of the senses.</note>.

### Chapter 44.

#### On Gentle Detachment,
#### True Contemplation, and Right Perfection.

In Christ JESUS, I wish that you desire to be satisfied, like Lazarus, by the crumbs of prayer of all the <term>Friends of God<note>In German, *Gottesfreunde*. Thus you shall find that which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, nor has ever

But **God** have mercy: one finds many ungrateful people who say: "Why should we concern ourselves with that which happened many years ago?"—meaning the suffering of our **Lord**—even though His wounds are in truth a living

<column-break/>

book and a bright mirror. Whoever enters into them rightly with **Saint Paul** <note>The Apostle Paul, who famously wrote of "bearing the marks of Jesus" and knowing nothing but "Christ crucified."</note> finds therein everything that the **Godhead** may bestow: the perfect opening of the seals of the living book. In this book one finds all perfection, in time and eternity, as Eternal Wisdom itself says: "I am the way, the truth, and the life." <note>original: *Ich bin der Weg/ die Warheit/ und das Leben*; quoting John 14:6.</note> Woe, and woe to all those who go another way.

The friends of **God** might weep blood that the noble wounds of **God** are so completely forgotten in all lands. We cannot be heard by our **Lord God** as long as we walk outside the fruit of His death. May the **Spirit of God** with all His rich gifts possess, quiet, and preserve you in **Christ Jesus**,
->Amen.<-

## CHAPTER XLVIII.
### Further concerning the sinking away of ourselves, and concerning the wounds of Christ.

IN Christ JESUS: **GOD** is such an incomprehensible Good that He may be grasped by no creature in time. For everything that the friends of **God** grasp in time, that is not **God**, but it is something *of* **God**, as **St. Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a theologian whose "apophatic" or negative theology taught that God is best known by realizing what He is NOT.</note> and **Gregory** <note>Likely St. Gregory the Great.</note> say: This is a dark cloud, which is above all senses and understanding, in which **Moses** was led by **God** upon the mountain. All friends of **God** chase after this; into this we must all be carried; for whatever freedom natural understanding brings forth in us, that perishes in eternal death. But what the heavenly Father brings forth in us, that grows fruitfully in eternal life, with detached silence, suffering, and upright thoughts.

---

<page-num>409</page-num>
<header>MARROW OF THE SOUL <note>original Latin: *MEDULLA ANIMÆ*</note>.</header>

We should pray to **God** that He give us strength, so that we may lay aside all selfhood: He is not wise who hopes for anything else than to dwell humbly in the honey-flowing <note>A common medieval metaphor describing the wounds of Christ as the source of spiritual sweetness and nourishment.</note> wounds of our **Lord**, in an indwelling of the truth, to be obedient in works of action and contemplation <note>Refers to the *vita activa* and *vita contemplativa*, the two traditional paths of Christian life.</note>, in everything in which one's will is tested outwardly and inwardly. We wish that **God** might answer you in all your well-doing in a swallowing <note>original: *verschlingender Weise*; this implies the soul being entirely consumed or absorbed by God's presence.</note> manner. Learn to remain with yourselves in all things, learn to let yourselves go, and practice yourselves at all times in gentleness and humility.

Offer yourselves at all times to the hidden **God**, in a manner of denying yourselves and all creatures, so that you may always be inwardly with the **Lord**. When one often thinks that they are of the very least use, that is when it is best, even if one does not perceive it. For nature must here stand altogether in true yieldedness <term>Gelassenheit: a central term in German mysticism meaning total surrender of the self-will and a peaceful detachment from worldly concerns.</term>.

A person who desires to be imprinted into the suffering and image of our **Lord**, he may boldly [offer himself] to the un-imaged... <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

### CHAPTER LII.

### DR. JOHN TAULER, THE MARROW OF THE SOUL.

I wish that the unspeakable love of **GOD**, with fiery thoughts of uniting you with Him, may completely pour through and sustain you. This is so that you may forget those things which are behind <note>A reference to Philippians 3:13</note>, leading to a disdain for yourselves and all creatures, and that you may compel yourselves toward and into the closest part of the inward man—into the abyss <term>Abgrund: a central term in German mysticism referring to the bottomless depth of God’s essence and the corresponding depth of the humble soul</term> of humility, purity, unity, and eternity.

And keep the outermost man <note>The "outer man" refers to the physical senses and worldly concerns, as opposed to the "inner man" of the spirit</note> closed off from all worry and the natural attachment of your own will, as well as from all the sorrow and pleasure of worldly fortune and misfortune. May the true Master Builder <note>original: *Werckmeister*, referring to God as the craftsman who shapes the soul</note>, who alone is capable of such a thing, work this in you and in me.

->**With fervor we shall walk the way of GOD.**<-

In **Christ JESUS**, may His countless, unspeakable, and gentle gifts be with you. 
O you most beloved sisters, learn in all

<column-break/>

all chastity and humility, to walk constantly, entirely purely, and fervently—which leads to the highest Good, and far surpasses everything that this world and its creatures can give. And turn your whole mind and desire with all your strength toward the heavenly life. This way is undertaken through the renunciation <note>original: *Abbrechung*, the cutting off or breaking away from worldly desires</note> of all pleasure, with the clearest and most unmixed intention; it is run through with hot desire, and is completed with the most burning love in fervent favor, and in an unspeakable taste of the countless goodness of **GOD**.

In this way, which exceeds all human power <note>original: *übergemöglichen Wege*, a path that is only possible through divine grace</note>, our old man dies <note>A Pauline concept referring to the unregenerate self dominated by pride and ego</note> with all his wisdom and perverted pride. And our new man is made living and transformed into the same likeness of the most imperishable Trinity of **GOD**. With all the love I am capable of, I ask you to pray through the same [Spirit], that He may lead us all together as one into and through the aforementioned way that lies before us—which is our **Lord JESUS Christ** Himself.

<summary>Tauler exhorts the sisters to withdraw from worldly attachments into the "abyss" of the inner man, where the soul is transformed into the likeness of the Trinity. He identifies this spiritual path as being found ultimately in the person of Jesus Christ.</summary>

## Through the Suffering of Christ We Come to Fiery Love.

To the handmaidens of Christ <note>A common address to a community of nuns, likely the Dominican sisters Tauler frequently counseled</note>, their servant sends a greeting to those whom they confess to be their salvation, joy, and desire—that they might heartily love Him with the innermost part of all their strength, He who is a Master of all blessedness. And that they may faithfully obey His commandments and counsel, and that they may quite humbly conform themselves to His holy image and suffering.

You handmaidens of Christ, what more should I write? For in these three pieces <note>Refers to the three points just mentioned: love for God, obedience to His word, and conformity to His suffering</note> the spirituality of all the saints and the practice of every person is contained. Whoever now stands more firmly within these, the closer they shall be found in **GOD**.

What can be lacking to one who truly loves Christ? For nothing is lacking to one who fears Him. And what does **GOD** demand more from us than that we surrender ourselves entirely to His commandment and teaching, and follow after His life and suffering? So that now

### How one may come to true love through the wounds of Jesus.

**IN** Christ **JESUS**: The soul’s grasping and knowing is situated in that one thing <note>likely a reference to the "one thing necessary" mentioned in Luke 10:42</note> which is necessary, so that we may practice it eternally with all the saints. ## An inward exercise in the wounds of our Lord.

Dear children in Christ Jesus: A soul that loves God should gaze upon and kiss His holy wounds; for the wounds of our Savior <note>original: *Seligmacher*—one who makes us blessed or brings salvation</note> give more beauty, joy, and clarity to the whole heavenly host than anything else that exists in eternal life under His Godhead.

Now, the God-loving person should, in this life, duly kiss the crowned head of our Lord. Through this, his spirit is transformed, and he becomes worthy of the Fatherly inheritance with Christ.

Secondly, one should look upon the wounds of the heart: thus the little soul <note>original: *Seelein*—a diminutive used to show endearment or the soul’s humility before God</note> receives a burning increase and love of all virtue.

Thirdly, one should gaze at the wound of the right hand; thus redemption, freedom, and the gentle grace of God are given to the person by God.

Fourthly, one should gaze at the wound of the left hand, from which begins the

This is a sure and true revelation from God, which has its foundation in the Holy Scripture of Jesus Christ.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.

->How we should carry the cross of our Lord in true yieldedness.<-

**I**n Christ Jesus, dear children: All disorder of the inner and outer man is set right through the yieldedness <note>original: *Gelassenheit*—a key term in German mysticism meaning a state of letting go, surrender, and detachment from self-will</note> of oneself under God in all His judgment and providence. Yes, in this yieldedness, the person is revealed to God and is carried by all creatures into the incomprehensible Good, which is God Himself. Therefore, take heed of yourselves, and of everything that God wants from you, and of the cross in which God wants to prepare you, and His most beloved will, so that you may possess the cell <note>original: *Klause*—traditionally a monk’s cell, here used metaphorically for the private space of the soul</note> of your heart in the use of God here in time and there in eternity. For the bitterer the cross is, the more joyful and noble the resurrection of the person in God will be afterward. Guard yourselves against specialized ways <note>The text breaks off here; the original *sonderlichen Weis* likely refers to "special wisdom" or "particular methods" of piety that can lead to pride.</note>

<summary>This page concludes a devotional meditation on the five wounds of Christ as sources of spiritual strength and begins a new discourse on Gelassenheit (yieldedness). Tauler explains that surrendering one's will to God's providence is the only way to reorder the soul and prepare it for eternal life.</summary>

### CHAPTER LXIII. <note>original: *CAPUT LXIII*</note>

#### Concerning the nine rocks <note>original: *neuen Felſen*; likely a printing variant of *neun* (nine), referring to a famous 14th-century mystical treatise, *The Book of the Nine Rocks*.</note> / or rungs / and how one should proceed through detachment <note>original: *Gelaſſenheit*; a central theme in German mysticism referring to the process of "letting go" of self-will to be completely yielded to God.</note> in a true Christian life.

In the book of the nine rocks, God revealed—in Tauler’s time—to one of his chosen friends <note>A reference to the "Friends of God" (*Gottesfreunde*), a medieval mystical movement of which Tauler was a leader.</note> how great and manifold sins have completely permeated the entire Christian order in all estates, so that people live very carelessly and without any fear of God. <meta>catchword: unless (original: dann)</meta>

<column-break/>

unless they desist from their great sins. 

But because few people improve themselves, it is to be feared that such previously mentioned plagues will come upon us.

In the aforementioned book of the nine rocks, God indicated nine estates <note>social or spiritual "stations" or "levels" of life.</note> in Christendom, in which alone those Christian people walk who live without mortal sins <term>mortal sins|Sins that are considered grave enough to sever the soul's relationship with God's grace.</term> and are set upon the way of salvation (toward their origin, which is God). All other people outside of these nine estates are children of eternal damnation, unless they convert in this time. But whoever hopes to be on one of these rungs should never stand still and cease from good works and exercises; rather, they should always walk forward with the improvement of their life in the love of God. For whoever stands still is soon driven back and brought into the snare and noose of the hellish enemy, with which he holds all people captive (except for those mentioned here). Yet this is not God’s fault, for God is ready for all people who [turn] from their sins with...

On the lowest step, or rungs of salvation, dwell those people who live in the fear of God and avoid all mortal sins.

This is the first approach to the likeness of God: for just as we turn away from God through sin, so we turn back to God through filial fear <note>A theological term for fear based on love and respect, like that of a child for a parent, rather than "servile fear" based on dread of punishment.</note>, by accepting His grace and virtue. They seek the comfort and pleasure of their senses and believe that one may serve God and Nature <note>In this context, "Nature" refers to the "fallen nature" or the desires of the flesh.</note> at the same time, and live well together in both, which is nonetheless very dangerous and can never endure. They are so free, untouched, and unconcerned in their <term>ground</term> <note>In Rhenish mysticism, the "ground" (Grund) refers to the deepest, most essential center of the soul where it meets God.</note> regarding all temporal goods—and even regarding the gifts of God and everything that is not purely God—as if they possessed nothing. They take their physical necessities (if they still have any) from their God without <term>self-attachment</term> <note>original: *Eygenschafft*. This technical term describes a sense of ownership or possessiveness over one's own will or spiritual state.</note>; the rest they share with God, to whom it all belongs anyway. These people have come very close to God; He holds them very dear and precious. He gives them great gifts and lets them see wonders, yet all in <term>images and forms</term> <note>Medieval theologians often distinguished between "images" (mental or sensory visions) and "essential" revelation, which is a direct, formless experience of God's essence.</note>. But commonly, the heights above essential revelation and the contemplation of God are hidden from them, for they have a secret, peering will that is not yet killed to its foundation. With this will, they accept the gifts of God very secretly, with a hidden self-attachment, so that they do not do without them as willingly as they receive them with total desire; and they do not recognize this themselves. But God well knows their secret ground, which still lies hidden in their nature, and He does not yet dare to fully trust them, such that he <margin>showed</margin> <note>original: *erzeigte*</note> <unclear>would withdraw</unclear> <note>original: ~~entzőge~~. man must remain so empty and free from all desires and self-attachment regarding all internal gifts—free in his heart—as if he had never received them. He must only marvel in true humility at the Divine, mild goodness toward the unworthy sinner, thanking and praising Him, and receiving all things from God and for God’s sake, and for no other "Why?" He must have a ready will to do without all gifts again and to stand in all suffering before he may ever reach his best state; for holiness does not lie in the gifts. Rather, God wants to show His sweet mildness through them, in order to lure weak people toward a perfect life.

All people of these eight previously described degrees still have failings and self-attachment in them—one more, the other less. And the higher the degree is, and the fewer people are found therein with a <term>lack of surrender</term> <note>original: *Ungelassenheit*. This is the opposite of *Gelassenheit* (releasement). ### DR. JOHANNES TAULER
<page-num>508</page-num>

A person who is in suffering or the peril of death should well consider and take these points to heart.

The first: he should go into himself and look at the cause of his suffering or affliction that torments him.

The second: he should from his heart admit his guilt in all suffering, and humbly confess before **GOD**, before men, and before his confessor <term>Beichtvatter: a spiritual guide to whom one confesses sins</term>, that he has deserved such through his sins.

The third: he should hold his suffering against the suffering of our **LORD** Jesus and examine how small the suffering of all men is compared to His.

The fourth: he should consider himself unworthy of the suffering and should thank **GOD** with his whole heart that He has deemed him worthy of His likeness; for **GOD** Himself was never without suffering, but willingly surrendered Himself to it, according to the most beloved will of His Father. Whoever comes to the **LORD** in this way with his suffering obtains five gifts.

The first is that **HE** forgives him all sins.

The fifth: that **GOD** gives him such great comfort that he can well do without the comfort of men.

# DR. JOHANNES TAULER
<page-num>516</page-num>

To die in **GOD**—it is a truly gentle thing to die in God’s will.

Among all good methods, thoughts, and devotions—however good they may be—when one is to die, none is so useful as to yield oneself entirely into God’s will. A person who dies completely and utterly in this state of yieldedness <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>A central concept in German mysticism meaning a total surrender of the self-will and a peaceful detachment from worldly things</note> would be saved in that very hour, without any doubt. And just as no mediator, pain, or purgatorial fire <note>original: "Creuß-feuers," literally "fire of the cross," referring to the trials or purifying sufferings of the soul</note> can enter into **GOD**, so too can none enter into the person who is thus united with **GOD** in love. There is also no safer way to die, nor a more perfect life to achieve great things, than solely through love to live in God’s will, and to leave all things to Him—in taking and in giving, with a pure intention toward **GOD**—and to seek oneself neither in time nor in eternity. This way surpasses all other ways.

These four ways belong to the friends of God; and those who were ready entered with the Bridegroom <note>An allusion to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25</note>—not those who only then wanted to prepare themselves; they remained outside, even though they ran to buy oil. ### CHAPTER 69.

->A beautiful preparation for a blessed death.<-

**First**, a dying person should turn away from all temporal things and, with all their strength and desires, turn to their heavenly Father in the promised land, seeking to be united with **GOD** there with great longing, and to thank and praise Him eternally for His great goodness.

**Second**, he should in no way rely on any good works that he has ever done, but with firm confidence, he should wrap himself alone in the worthy suffering <term>Leyden</term> and merit of our Lord **Jesus Christ**. He should sink himself—along with all his sins and omissions—into the deep sea of His bottomless mercy, as well as into His holy wounds. ### VII.

**On verse 6. Sprinkle me with hyssop.** <note>original: "Super vers. 6. Besprenge mich mit Ysopen." Hyssop was used in ancient purification rituals.</note> Just as the sprinkling with hyssop / and washing with water outwardly / is not useful / for the inner washing and sprinkling / except only as a figure and a mere sign: Likewise also all other outward ways and gestures / which intend nothing else / than that in like manner **GOD** should inwardly sprinkle / wash / work / speak / care for / etc. with the grace of the **Holy Spirit** / and thus the dear old Fathers viewed the figures in the Old Testament / and understood beneath them the inner and hidden part of the true understanding and the wisdom of **God**.
