### IX.

On Psalm 102, verse 5. **I have forgotten to eat my bread.** The bread of the dry <note>The "dry heart" refers to a state of spiritual desolation or "aridity" where one feels no emotional connection to God.</note> heart is no one but God Himself, who alone can feed the hearts; for the heart must have an eternal food if it is to be satisfied.

### X.

On Psalm 130, verse 3. **If you should mark sins.** <note>Original: "So du wilt Sünde zurechnen." This is a translation of the Latin *Si iniquitates observaveris*.</note> In a righteous person, there must always be fear before the judgment of God because of the **old man**, <note>The "old man" is a Pauline term for the unregenerate, selfish human nature inherited from Adam.</note> whom God hates and opposes. And alongside this fear, there must be hope for grace and mercy, which is favorable to that very fear, for the sake of the **new man**, who is also an enemy to the old man and thus agrees with God’s judgment, etc.

### XI.

On verse 5. **I hope in His word.** This is the nature of the inward and new man: that he maintains a constant waiting, hoping, trusting, and believing in God; therefore, God does not abandon him.

<column-break/>

### XII. <note>This heading number is provided by the catchword on the previous page.</note>

On verse 6. **My soul waits for the Lord, from one morning watch to the next, etc.** The new man, whose work is nothing other than waiting for God and attending to Him, shall not cease, as the outer man does and must do. <note>The "outer man" refers to the physical body and its worldly duties, which require rest and change, unlike the spirit.</note> And this is the life in the three high virtues—**Faith, Hope, and Love**—etc. In this little Psalm, the entire life, work, and conduct of the inward man is masterfully described: that it is nothing other than a surrender to God and remaining completely resigned to God’s will.

### XIII.

In the conclusion of these Penitential Psalms. <note>These are a specific collection of seven Psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143) traditionally used to express sorrow for sin.</note> Christ Jesus is God’s grace, mercy, righteousness, truth, wisdom, strength, comfort, and salvation, given to us by God without any merit. Christ, I say—not (as some say with blind words) **causally**, <note>Original: *causaliter*. This is a critique of scholastic theologians who argued that Christ causes righteousness to happen in a person while remaining distant or separate from them.</note> which would mean that He gives righteousness but remains on the outside; for that righteousness is dead—indeed, it is never truly given unless Christ Himself is also present.

<summary>This page concludes the commentary on the Penitential Psalms, emphasizing that spiritual satisfaction comes only from God and that the "new man" lives in a state of constant, hopeful waiting. It argues for the "mystical union," claiming that Christ’s righteousness cannot be separated from His actual presence within the believer.</summary>

### LI.

The Scripture divides man into
three parts: **Spirit, Soul, and Body:**
the first part, the Spirit, is the highest and
noblest part of man (this is what Tauler calls
the pure essence of the soul) through
which he is capable of grasping
incomprehensible, invisible, and eternal things;
and it is truly the house in which
faith and the Word of God have their
seat. The second, the Soul, is the
same Spirit according to nature, but yet in
a different function. The Spirit is the
Holy of Holies, the dwelling of God, in
the hidden and, as it were, the darkness, etc.
*On the Magnificat* <note>original: "Super Magnif." This refers to Martin Luther's commentary on the Magnificat (the Song of Mary).</note>.

# Appendix

Johannes Tauler directed all his sermons (and also this little book) toward such a reformation (of our Adamite, fleshly heart), and for this purpose he used God’s Word as the most glorious and best means. He interprets this Word in such a way that he first opens and carries out from it the fleshly and sinful state, and thereafter the improvement of the same, with a special, high spiritual understanding and devotion; one can visibly perceive the power and working of the Holy Spirit in his speaking. Whoever does not understand the qualities of the Spirit of God in the interpretation of Holy Scripture, stumbles in with his fleshly <term>judgment <note>original: "Judicio." Arnd is criticizing those who use human logic rather than spiritual insight.</note></term> and

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>471</page-num>
<header>THE MARROW OF THE SOUL</header>

and judgment in this way: As "N." <note>A common placeholder in early modern texts for an unnamed person or opponent.</note> writes in a letter: "Whoever uses such a manner of speaking (as Tauler does) has drawn it from the <term>cisterns of monks <note>original: "Lacunis Monachorum." This was a derogatory term used by critics to imply that mystical ideas were just stagnant, stale inventions of monasteries rather than fresh biblical truth.</note></term>." Oh no, dear fellow, they are not "cisterns of monks," but it is the Holy Spirit’s <term>style <note>original: "Stylus."</note></term> and way of speaking thus. It will remain ungrasped by those fleshly, world-addicted spirits who place and ground everything upon eloquence, the elegance of languages, and the judgment of human reason. It has unfortunately come to the point that Holy Scripture is interpreted more according to the flesh and reason than according to the Spirit, and Theology is made more into a rational art than a Divine teaching and illumination. Tauler grounds his entire teaching on the subduing of the flesh and the raising up of the spirit, or the "new man," and teaches the heart to surrender to God alone. He names this with an old German word (common in his time) called <term>Gelassenheit <note>This central concept of German mysticism refers to a state of "yieldedness," "releasement," or "letting go" of one's own will to make room for God.</note></term>: And it is nothing other than letting oneself into the will of God, leaving the world, clinging to God with the whole heart, and oneself...

<summary>In this appendix, Johann Arnd defends the 14th-century mystic Johannes Tauler, arguing that Tauler's specialized spiritual language is divinely inspired rather than merely "monkish." Arnd contrasts spiritual illumination with the dry, rationalistic theology of his own day, highlighting the core concept of Gelassenheit (yieldedness to God).</summary>
